title: Pencil grades: what do H, B and HB actually mean?
description: The tiny letters on your pencil explain its mark. Decode H, B, HB, 2H and 2B without turning your desk into an art shop.

cover.alt: Three sharpened wooden graphite pencils beside light, medium and dark graphite swatches on cream paper

sections.title: The letters are doing a small job
sections.html:
H means hard, B means black, and HB means hard black. In the usual graphite pencil scale, H grades are harder, B grades are softer and darker, and HB sits between them. Pencil maker STAEDTLER explains the letters and grades.

A pencil looks like such a simple object that its tiny code can seem oddly serious. You wanted to draw a cat, not choose a spacecraft component. Fortunately, the code is just a clue to the kind of mark it makes.

sections.title: Why 2H and 2B go in different directions
sections.html:
A larger number before H means a harder grade: 2H is harder than H. A larger number before B means a softer grade: 2B is softer than B.

So the number is not a quality score. A 4H pencil has not beaten a 2B pencil in a competition. They do different jobs. Softer grades help with dark shading; harder grades suit lighter, finer work. STAEDTLER groups its grades by writing and drawing uses.

sections.title: What changes inside the pencil?
sections.html:
In a traditional graphite pencil, the core contains graphite and clay. Graphite leaves the familiar grey-black mark. According to STAEDTLER’s manufacturing explanation, changing their proportions changes the hardness: more clay makes a harder core; more graphite makes it softer and blacker.

The barrel colour can be cheerful, but it does not tell you the grade. The little H or B is the useful clue when two ordinary pencils leave surprisingly different marks.

sections.title: Try three patches on scrap paper
sections.html:
If you have an H, an HB and a B pencil, shade a small patch with each using similar pressure. Compare the marks. A darker patch does not automatically mean a better pencil; it might simply be closer to the effect you want.

Remember the two directions: more H, harder; more B, softer. You can return to drawing the cat. Its dramatic shadow may need a different pencil from its first faint outline.
